findings.quote: if $5.46 is a blended network number and Alder & Vance actually ships heavier, more expensive parcels, then this chart is flattering them and I've been handed the bad end of an average
If slow movers are three percent of my lines then 17% of them is a rounding error and I don't want a task force.
we're looking at a chart whose most expensive bars are two percent of the business - that belongs on the chart, not underneath it
we're a fraction of a company against a whole company and the comparison flatters us badly

This is "both banners" - one blended number. Off-Main runs a different assortment with different depth, and I'd bet money our order fill sits below the blend and Alder & Vance sits above it, and this chart lets that hide.
Five of the seven headline numbers are not on their plots.
the $4 point is dropped off the plot and only mentioned in the note, which stopped me for a second while I worked out why the line starts at $5
the sector is rendered as a static band with no time dimension at all
If primary means Fernhill, double is $4.54 and no store clears it - claim false.
The gaps between ticks aren't equal so the slope of the fall is distorted, and the steepest-looking drop between $6 and $7 might just be the spacing.
two solid same-weight lines converging, hue-only
the achieved unit-fill series is gold in chart 1 and green in chart 2. A reader moving between the two will not recognize it as the same series.
a non-round top tick jammed against the last regular one. It reads as a bug, not a decision.
the title rounds 3.55% to "4%" while the label on the bar says 3.55%. A reader comparing title to label sees 4 vs 3.5.
The "Alder & Vance" in-plot label sits directly on top of the green line near $6-$7; the text and the line overlap.
The bottom annotation's second line, "series does," runs into the 0.0 gridline and axis labels.

Three category points with two co-rising series is co-movement, nothing more. The in-plot annotation states "one cause, thin fragmented stock" as fact. That's the weakest link in the chart, and it's asserted twice.
"Uses two nodes" reads at first glance as a label for B's blue bar specifically rather than for the blue series. I looked twice at that.

The descriptive paragraph appears above the title in every image, so a sighted reader gets a flat summary of the axes before reaching the headline sentence. If that text is meant for screen readers only, it's leaking into the visual render.
Store 104 and Store 103 are both $4.12 and drawn at identical height, presented inside an ordered ranking with no indication it's a tie
This is a service-benefit chart with no cost axis
the whole thing sits on a 73-99 axis, so the peak troughs look more dramatic than a 100-scale would show
it's a very thin chart - two bars, both labelled, is a sentence with axes
I'd also want cost per order rather than per unit, since store shipments tend to be one-liners.
the subtitle admits the counterfactual is "evaluated on the inventory position before each allocation," which I don't fully follow on first read
